title: Early Islamic Iraq
subtitle: 632–945 · Kufa, Basra and the New City of Baghdad — the Garrison Towns, the Sawad at Its Height, the Making of Sunni and Shia Iraq, and the World Capital of the Abbasids

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The conquest and the garrison cities, Kufa the capital of Ali and the home of dissent, al-Hajjaj and the Umayyad grip, the Abbasid Revolution coming from Kufa, al-Mansur's Baghdad, the golden age, Samarra and the Turks, and power passing to the wazirs and the amir al-umara

entries.group: The Caliphs and Governors in Iraq
entries.label: The conquest and the founding of Kufa and Basra
entries.hint: Within two years of al-Qadisiyya the Arab armies laid out two garrison cities on the desert edge — Basra near the head of the Gulf, Kufa near the ruins of al-Hira — as bases from which to hold the Sawad and push into Iran. They filled with tribesmen drawing a state stipend, and within a generation they were the two largest and most turbulent cities of the Muslim world.
entries.note: al-Baladhuri, 'Futūḥ al-Buldān'; al-Tabari I; Hichem Djaït, 'Al-Kūfa: naissance de la ville islamique' (1986).

entries.group: The Caliphs and Governors in Iraq
entries.label: Kufa the capital of Ali and the home of dissent
entries.hint: Ali moved the caliphate to Kufa in 656 and was murdered in its mosque five years later. The city stayed the centre of loyalty to his house and of every grievance against Damascus: it invited al-Husayn to his death at Karbala, rose for the Penitents and then for al-Mukhtar, and gave the Umayyads' governors their hardest problem for the next sixty years.
entries.note: al-Tabari II; Wilferd Madelung, 'The Succession to Muhammad' (1997).

entries.group: The Caliphs and Governors in Iraq
entries.label: al-Hajjaj and the Umayyad grip
entries.hint: The Umayyads ruled Iraq through hard men — Ziyad ibn Abihi, then al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, who governed for twenty years by terror. He broke the great revolt of the Iraqi army under Ibn al-Ash'ath, built a fresh garrison city, Wasit, midway between Kufa and Basra to hold Syrian troops apart from the Iraqis, and reformed the coinage and the canals. Iraq paid, and hated him.
entries.note: al-Tabari II; al-Baladhuri, 'Ansāb al-Ashrāf'; the foundation of Wasit in Yāqūt.

entries.group: The Caliphs and Governors in Iraq
entries.label: The Abbasids come to power from Kufa
entries.hint: The revolution that overthrew the Umayyads was made in Khurasan but proclaimed in Iraq: in October 749 the Abbasid Abu al-Abbas was hailed as caliph in the mosque of Kufa. His brother al-Mansur, who really built the dynasty, distrusted the Kufans as much as any Umayyad had, and looked for a capital of his own.
entries.note: al-Tabari III; Hugh Kennedy, 'The Early Abbasid Caliphate' (1981).

entries.group: The Caliphs and Governors in Iraq
entries.label: al-Mansur builds Baghdad
entries.hint: In 762 al-Mansur laid out a perfectly round walled city on the west bank of the Tigris, a few miles up from the ruins of Ctesiphon, and named it the City of Peace. The palace and the great mosque stood at the centre, the four gates faced the four roads of the empire, and within fifty years the built-up area had spilled far beyond the walls into the largest city west of China.
entries.note: al-Ya'qubi, 'Kitāb al-Buldān'; al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, 'Ta'rīkh Baghdād'; Jacob Lassner, 'The Topography of Baghdad in the Early Middle Ages' (1970).

entries.group: The Caliphs and Governors in Iraq
entries.label: The golden age and the war for Baghdad
entries.hint: Under Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun the city was the hub of the world's wealth and learning — and then, in 812–813, the arena of a year-long siege, as al-Ma'mun's armies from the east stormed the capital of his brother al-Amin, who was caught and killed. Al-Ma'mun stayed away for six years and came back to a city that had begun its long habit of destroying itself.
entries.note: al-Tabari III; the siege poems of al-Khuraymi; Michael Cooperson, 'Al-Maʾmun' (2005).

entries.group: The Caliphs and Governors in Iraq
entries.label: al-Mu'tasim, the Turks and Samarra
entries.hint: To house a new army of Turkish and Central Asian slave-soldiers apart from a resentful Baghdad, al-Mu'tasim built a second capital sixty miles up the Tigris at Samarra in 836. It became a byword for the state's captivity to its own guard: between 861 and 870 the soldiers murdered four caliphs in a decade. The court returned to Baghdad in 892, leaving Samarra to shrink back to a village.
entries.note: al-Ya'qubi, 'Kitāb al-Buldān'; Matthew Gordon, 'The Breaking of a Thousand Swords' (2001); Alastair Northedge, 'The Historical Topography of Samarra' (2005).

entries.label: Power passes to the wazirs and the amir al-umara
entries.hint: After a brief recovery under al-Mu'tadid the caliphate ran out of money and out of soldiers it could trust. Rival bureaucratic clans fought over the vizierate; then in 936 the office of amir al-umara, commander of commanders, handed real power to whichever general held Baghdad. In December 945 that general was a Buyid from the Caspian, and the caliph became his pensioner.
entries.note: Miskawayh, 'Tajārib al-Umam'; Harold Bowen, 'The Life and Times of ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā' (1928).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Camel and Siffin fought from Iraq, Karbala and the Kufan risings, Ibn al-Ash'ath and the army's revolt against al-Hajjaj, the siege of Baghdad in the war of the brothers, the fourteen-year Zanj rebellion in the marshes, and the Qaramita

entries.label: The Camel, Siffin and Nahrawan
entries.hint: The first war among Muslims was fought largely on Iraqi ground. Ali beat a rival army outside Basra at the Battle of the Camel in 656, faced Mu'awiya's Syrians to a standstill at Siffin on the upper Euphrates in 657, and then turned on his own hardliners — the first Kharijites — and destroyed them at Nahrawan near the future Baghdad in 658. Iraq was left permanently split.
entries.note: al-Tabari I; al-Minqari, 'Waqʿat Ṣiffīn'; Wilferd Madelung (1997).

entries.label: Karbala and the Kufan revolts
entries.hint: Invited by the Kufans and then abandoned by them, the Prophet's grandson al-Husayn was surrounded and killed with his small party on the plain of Karbala on the tenth of Muharram, 680. The guilt of it drove two Kufan risings within a decade — the Penitents, and then al-Mukhtar's movement in the name of another son of Ali — and made martyrdom and the pilgrimage to the grave the core of Shia devotion.
entries.note: al-Tabari II; Abu Mikhnaf's 'Maqtal al-Ḥusayn'; Mahmoud Ayoub, 'Redemptive Suffering in Islam' (1978).

entries.label: Ibn al-Ash'ath and the army's revolt
entries.hint: Sent east to fight in Sistan, the Iraqi army turned around, marched home, and rose against al-Hajjaj and the Umayyad state — joined by many of the Quran-reciters and jurists of Kufa and Basra. Al-Hajjaj broke them at Dayr al-Jamajim in 701 with Syrian troops and then hunted the leaders down. It was the last time the old Iraqi military class tried to set the terms of its own service.
entries.note: al-Tabari II; Redwan Sayed, 'Die Revolte des Ibn al-Ashʿath' (1977).

entries.label: The siege of Baghdad
entries.hint: When the brothers al-Amin and al-Ma'mun fell out, al-Ma'mun's Khurasani general Tahir besieged the capital for more than a year. Catapults battered the round city, the suburbs burned, and irregular bands of the poor — the 'naked ones' — did much of the fighting for al-Amin. He was taken trying to flee across the river and killed. It was the first sack of Baghdad, by its own empire.
entries.note: al-Tabari III; the eyewitness verses of al-Khuraymi in al-Ṭabari; John Nawas on the civil war.

entries.label: The Zanj rebellion in the marshes
entries.hint: East African slaves cutting the nitrous crust off the salt flats of lower Iraq for wages that never came rose in 869 under a man who claimed descent from Ali. For fourteen years they held the marshes, built a capital, minted coins, sacked Basra in 871 with great slaughter, and threatened Baghdad. The regent al-Muwaffaq finally ground them down in 883. It was the largest slave revolt before modern times.
entries.note: al-Tabari III; Alexandre Popović, 'The Revolt of African Slaves in Iraq' (1999).

entries.label: The Qaramita and the helpless caliphate
entries.hint: An Ismaili preacher organised the peasants of the Sawad around Kufa in the 870s; the movement built a raiding state on the Gulf coast that in the 900s cut the pilgrim roads, defeated caliphal armies, and in 930 stormed Mecca during the hajj, massacred the pilgrims, and carried off the Black Stone. That the caliphate could do nothing about it for twenty years measured how far it had fallen.
entries.note: al-Tabari III; Miskawayh; Wilferd Madelung, 'Fatimiden und Bahrainqarmaten' (1959).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The garrison cities and the stipend register, the land and tax of the Sawad kept from the Sasanians, Baghdad as the imperial capital, the wazirate and the diwans, the qadi and the rise of Islamic law, and the protected communities under the caliph

entries.label: The amsar and the stipend register
entries.hint: Kufa and Basra began as tribal cantonments — quarters assigned by clan, a governor's residence and a mosque at the centre, and a register, the diwan, that paid every fighting man an annual stipend graded by precedence in Islam. The stipend, not land, was the reward of conquest. As the money and the tribesmen settled, the camps hardened into cities of a quarter-million and more.
entries.note: al-Baladhuri, 'Futūḥ al-Buldān'; Fred Donner, 'The Early Islamic Conquests' (1981); Hichem Djaït (1986).

entries.label: The Sawad kept as a common endowment
entries.hint: The caliph Umar refused to divide the conquered farmland of the Sawad among the soldiers; it was left with its cultivators as fayʾ, a permanent endowment for the whole community, taxed by the Sasanian survey the conquerors had inherited. The old crown estates became the caliph's sawafi. Al-Hajjaj later tried to pin the peasants to the land and tax converts like everyone else — a policy that helped make Iraq ungovernable.
entries.note: Abu Yusuf, 'Kitāb al-Kharāj'; Michael Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984).

entries.label: Baghdad as the machine of empire
entries.hint: The imperial capital ran on a dense apparatus: the caliphal palace-cities on both banks, the chief judge over a network of qadis, the market inspector policing weights and morals, the police, the postmaster who was also the caliph's spy, and a treasury drawing on the revenue of three continents. Feeding and ordering a city of half a million was itself a feat of government.
entries.note: al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, 'Ta'rīkh Baghdād'; Jacob Lassner, 'The Shaping of ʿAbbāsid Rule' (1980).

entries.label: The wazirate and the diwans
entries.hint: The Abbasids ran their empire through a vizier and a set of ministries — land tax, army, chancery, seal, posts — staffed by a professional secretarial class, the kuttab, largely of Persian and Christian background and trained in an Iranian tradition of statecraft. The Barmakid family, viziers for a generation under Harun al-Rashid, showed both the reach of the office and how fast a caliph could destroy its holders.
entries.note: al-Jahshiyari, 'Kitāb al-Wuzarāʾ wa-l-Kuttāb'; Dominique Sourdel, 'Le vizirat ʿabbāside' (1959).

entries.label: The qadi and the making of fiqh
entries.hint: Early on a judge decided by the governor's instructions and his own sense of right. Over two generations the jurists of Kufa and Basra turned that into a system — a body of reasoned law with its own methods and its own teachers. Abu Hanifa and his students in Kufa, working by analogy and considered opinion, produced the first great school; the writing-down of law had begun.
entries.note: al-Shaybani, 'Kitāb al-Aṣl'; Joseph Schacht, 'The Origins of Muhammadan Jurisprudence' (1950); Wael Hallaq, 'The Origins and Evolution of Islamic Law' (2005).

entries.label: The dhimma and its communal heads
entries.hint: Jews, Christians, Mandaeans and Zoroastrians lived as protected non-Muslims — paying the poll tax, barred from certain offices and dress, but self-governing under leaders the caliph recognised by diploma: the exilarch for the Jews, the catholicos for the Church of the East. The arrangement continued the Sasanian pattern. It could tighten sharply, as under al-Mutawakkil's edicts of 850.
entries.note: al-Tabari III (al-Mutawakkil's edicts); Milka Levy-Rubin, 'Non-Muslims in the Early Islamic Empire' (2011).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Iraqi schools of law at Kufa and Basra, the traditionists and the isnad, the birth of Shia Islam at Kufa and Karbala and the shrine cities, the Mutazila and the Inquisition, the geonim and the Nestorian catholicos at their height, and the first Sufis

entries.label: Kufa, Basra and the birth of the madhhab
entries.hint: The two garrison cities became the two poles of early Islamic legal thought. Kufa was the home of raʾy — disciplined reasoned opinion, worked out from principle where the texts ran short — and of Abu Hanifa, whose circle produced the first school to outlast its founder. The habit of arguing law in named, competing traditions, the madhhab system, starts here.
entries.note: Nurit Tsafrir, 'The History of an Islamic School of Law: The Early Spread of Hanafism' (2004); Christopher Melchert, 'The Formation of the Sunni Schools of Law' (1997).

entries.label: The traditionists and the isnad
entries.hint: Against the reasoners rose the people of hadith, who held that the only sound guide beyond the Quran was an authenticated report of what the Prophet said or did, each carried by a named chain of transmitters back to an eyewitness. Basra was a great centre of the collecting and the sifting, and of the vast biographical science that grew up to judge which transmitters could be trusted.
entries.note: Jonathan Brown, 'Hadith: Muhammad's Legacy in the Medieval and Modern World' (2009).

entries.label: The shrines and the Occultation
entries.hint: Shia Islam grew up in the soil of Kufa. Over these centuries its holy geography took form on Iraqi ground: the grave of Ali at Najaf, identified in the late 700s; Karbala, where al-Husayn fell; the tombs of two imams at al-Kazimayn in Baghdad; and Samarra, where the eleventh imam died and the twelfth was said to have gone into hiding in 874, and then into a total concealment in 941 that still holds.
entries.note: Heinz Halm, 'Shiʿism' (1991); Moojan Momen, 'An Introduction to Shiʿi Islam' (1985).

entries.label: The Mutazila and the Inquisition
entries.hint: A school of theologians that began in Basra held that reason could establish God's justice and unity — and that the Quran, being an act of God rather than a part of him, was created in time. In 833 al-Ma'mun made assent to the created Quran a test of office and imprisoned those who refused, Ahmad ibn Hanbal chief among them. The Inquisition failed; when it was lifted in 848 the traditionists had won the argument in the street.
entries.note: al-Tabari III; Josef van Ess, 'Theologie und Gesellschaft' (1991–97); John Nawas on the mihna.

entries.label: The geonim and the catholicos at their height
entries.hint: With the court at Baghdad the two great institutions of the protected faiths reached their peak there. The Jewish academies of Sura and Pumbedita, now in the capital, sent legal rulings to communities from Spain to India, and Saadia Gaon translated the Bible into Arabic and beat back the Karaite challenge. The Nestorian patriarch Timothy I debated theology with al-Mahdi and dispatched bishops toward China.
entries.note: Robert Brody, 'The Geonim of Babylonia' (1998); the 'Apology of Timothy'; Sebastian Brock (2000).

entries.label: From the Basran ascetics to al-Hallaj
entries.hint: Muslim mysticism took shape in Iraq. It began with the fear-filled asceticism of al-Hasan al-Basri's Basra and Rabiʿa's teaching of pure love of God, and matured in Baghdad into a disciplined path — al-Junayd's careful, 'sober' Sufism. Its limit was tested by al-Hallaj, who spoke of union with God in the first person and was crucified in Baghdad in 922.
entries.note: Louis Massignon, 'The Passion of al-Hallāj' (tr. 1982); Ahmet Karamustafa, 'Sufism: The Formative Period' (2007).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Arabic grammar codified at Basra and Kufa, the adab golden age and the poets of the Baghdad court, paper and the booksellers' market, the Round City and the Samarra style, and the singing-girls and the legend of Harun's Baghdad

entries.label: The grammarians of Basra and Kufa
entries.hint: As Arabic became the language of a non-Arab empire, scholars in the two garrison cities set out to fix its rules. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad of Basra compiled the first dictionary and codified the metres of poetry; his Persian pupil Sibawayh wrote a grammar so complete it was simply called The Book. The Kufan school challenged the Basrans point by point, and out of the quarrel came classical Arabic.
entries.note: Sibawayh, 'al-Kitāb'; Michael Carter, 'Sibawayhi' (2004); the Basra–Kufa debate in al-Anbari's 'al-Inṣāf'.

entries.label: Adab and the prose of the salon
entries.hint: A new kind of writing — witty, digressive, encyclopedic, meant to make a cultivated man good company — took shape in Abbasid Iraq. Ibn al-Muqaffa turned the Persian mirror-for-princes and the Indian fable book into Arabic prose; al-Jahiz of Basra wrote on everything from misers to the anatomy of animals with the same restless irony. This adab set the standard of educated Arabic for a thousand years.
entries.note: al-Jahiz, 'Kitāb al-Ḥayawān' and 'al-Bukhalāʾ'; Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, 'Kalīla wa-Dimna'.

entries.label: The poets of the Baghdad court
entries.hint: The court and its patrons drew the best poets of the age to Baghdad, and they broke with the desert conventions: Abu Nuwas made wine, the city and self-mockery into high art; Abu Tammam and al-Buhturi built the ornate badiʿ style of dense metaphor. Poetry was a career — a good ode could be worth a fortune — and the caliph's praise or displeasure made and ruined reputations.
entries.note: the 'Dīwān' of Abu Nuwas; Suzanne Stetkevych, 'Abū Tammām and the Poetics of the ʿAbbāsid Age' (1991).

entries.label: Paper, the warraqin and the book trade
entries.hint: Paper reached Baghdad from Samarkand and the first mill opened around 795; within a century the trade in books had a street of its own, the Market of the Stationers near the Basra Gate, where copyists sold, authors dictated, and scholars met. The bookseller Ibn al-Nadim's catalogue of everything then available in Arabic lists thousands of titles. No pre-modern society produced books on this scale.
entries.note: Ibn al-Nadim, 'al-Fihrist'; Jonathan Bloom, 'Paper Before Print' (2001).

entries.label: The Round City and the Samarra style
entries.hint: Al-Mansur's Baghdad was a perfect circle, a plan with no real precedent or sequel, its palace and mosque ringed by two miles of double wall. Samarra was the opposite — a strip city thirty kilometres long, its Great Mosque fronted by the spiral Malwiya minaret, its palaces sheathed in moulded stucco cut in a slanted, endlessly repeatable pattern. That Samarra style travelled from Egypt to Central Asia.
entries.note: Alastair Northedge, 'The Historical Topography of Samarra' (2005); Jacob Lassner, 'The Topography of Baghdad' (1970).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The translation movement and the House of Wisdom, al-Kindi and the first Arabic philosophy, al-Khwarizmi and the exact sciences, the Baghdad hospital and the physicians, and rational theology as a system

entries.label: Greek learning into Arabic
entries.hint: Over four generations nearly the whole of Greek science and philosophy that survived was turned into Arabic, mostly through Syriac, by teams of salaried translators — the Christian physician Hunayn ibn Ishaq's workshop the most exacting of them. Caliphs, viziers and rich families paid for it, sometimes by the weight of the finished book. It was a sustained public project, not a scattering of curiosity.
entries.note: Dimitri Gutas, 'Greek Thought, Arabic Culture' (1998); the 'Risāla' of Hunayn ibn Ishaq on his Galen translations.

entries.label: al-Kindi and the first Arabic philosophy
entries.hint: Al-Kindi, an Arab nobleman at the courts of al-Ma'mun and al-Mu'tasim, was the first to do philosophy in Arabic — arguing that the truths of Greek metaphysics and of revelation were one, and writing on optics, music, medicine, cryptanalysis and the making of perfumes besides. He set the pattern of the Muslim philosopher as a universal scientist working under a patron.
entries.note: al-Kindi, 'On First Philosophy'; Peter Adamson, 'Al-Kindī' (2007).

entries.label: al-Khwarizmi and the sciences of number
entries.hint: Working in al-Ma'mun's circle, al-Khwarizmi wrote the book that named and founded algebra, a treatise that carried the Indian decimal numerals into the Arabic world — and, through a Latin garble of his name, gave Europe the word algorithm — and a set of astronomical tables blending Indian and Greek method. Alongside him the Banu Musa brothers worked on geometry and machines.
entries.note: al-Khwarizmi, 'al-Kitāb al-mukhtaṣar fī ḥisāb al-jabr wa-l-muqābala'; Roshdi Rashed, 'Al-Khwārizmī: The Beginnings of Algebra' (2009).

entries.label: Medicine and the Baghdad hospital
entries.hint: The physicians of Gondeshapur came to court with the Abbasids, and around 805 a hospital on the Persian model was built in Baghdad under Barmakid patronage — a teaching institution with wards, a pharmacy and a staff. Hunayn's translations gave Arabic the whole Galenic corpus; a century later al-Razi, directing a Baghdad hospital, added a lifetime of case notes and clinical judgement.
entries.note: Ibn Abi Usaybia, 'ʿUyūn al-Anbāʾ'; al-Razi, 'al-Ḥāwī'; Peter Pormann & Emilie Savage-Smith, 'Medieval Islamic Medicine' (2007).

entries.label: History and geography become disciplines
entries.hint: Baghdad's scholars invented the large-scale forms of both fields. Al-Tabari compiled a history of the world from the creation to his own day, year by year, quoting his sources; al-Baladhuri wrote the story of the conquests; and the postmaster Ibn Khurradadhbih turned his official knowledge of the roads and revenues into the first Arabic geography of routes. History and geography were now organised sciences with methods.
entries.note: al-Tabari, 'Ta'rīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk'; Ibn Khurradadhbih, 'Kitāb al-Masālik wa-l-Mamālik'; Chase Robinson, 'Islamic Historiography' (2003).
